St. Flavian of Constantinople

Saint Flavian of Constantinople

St. Flavian of Constantinople · St. Flavian the Confessor · St. Flavianos of Constantinople

Period
Fifth century; died 449
Region
Constantinople; Ephesus
Titles / vocation
Hierarch · Confessor
Commemoration
February 18

Introduction

Saint Flavian was Patriarch of Constantinople and an opponent of Eutyches. He suffered violence at the Ephesus assembly of 449 and died soon afterward.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Died after severe council violence in 449; the OCA honors him as Confessor

Read circumstances and sources

Background

Before becoming patriarch he was a priest and caretaker of church vessels in Constantinople’s cathedral. He succeeded Patriarch Proclus during a period of conflict over how to confess Christ’s divinity and humanity.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Opening paragraphs on presbyteral service and succession

Life and notable events

In 448 he convened a local council to examine Eutyches’ teaching. The next year a council at Ephesus reinstated Eutyches and condemned Saint Flavian through intimidation and force. Orthodox sources call this assembly the Robber Council, distinguishing it from an Ecumenical Council.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Paragraphs on448local council and449Ephesusassembly

Death and martyrdom

The OCA describes severe beatings, imprisonment in chains, and a sentence of banishment before his death in August 449. It honors him with the title Confessor. His death followed the persecution described in the account.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Final paragraphs on beating, chains, exile and death

The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese’s life of his successor explicitly attributes Saint Flavian’s death to the beatings he received.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Opening reading paragraph on449

Writings and legacy

His opposition to Eutyches forms part of the conflict preceding Chalcedon. Saint Pulcheria later arranged the return of his relics to Constantinople. His commemoration preserves the distinction between an assembly’s political power and its reception by the Church.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Opening doctrinal context and final paragraph on transfer of relics
